I will undress you, and you will undress me (...) You see how this looks, right?I saw this film a few days ago (I'm writing this on Thursday 26th) and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since. 

As we all know, Primetime is based on the real-life case of the show To Catch a Predator. Despite this, it's quite fictional, so I think many of the situations it portrays are still relevant today and make us wonder if we're progressing as a society or if we're worse off now. 

This film shows how different types of predators operate. Yes, the first thing that comes to mind is pedophiles, but it goes even further by showing how Chris manipulated Dan, taking advantage of his greater age and position of power, which highlights non-sexual grooming (if you can even call it that, considering Dan was already an adult, lol).

I found the portrayal of Chris interesting. For many, he was a hero, but in his private life he had internal conflicts that, if revealed, would completely tarnish his image, and he would hate that. A lot of people didn't like the movie because they say it supposedly portrays him as the villain, but I don't think that's the case. Chris simply couldn't completely eliminate the evil that has always existed in this world, not even the evil within himself. 

Regarding the characters, I really loved Dan. I thought it was sweet that they tried to represent all the paid actors who participated in Predator. As one of his friends told Dan, he wouldn't normally have paid attention to his role if he were just an ordinary viewer, but the reality is that these actors played a fundamental part in the show. The good thing is that in the end, Dan was able to fulfill his dream.

 Something I really appreciated was the use of visuals. The fact that the quality deteriorated more and more as the film progressed added a lot to the dense nature of this story. Furthermore, everyone's acting was super realistic.

 I didn't give it 5 stars because in some parts it felt a little empty (to put it mildly) and because the issue of Chris's family was left unresolved. We'll see if my opinion changes once I see it again in theaters (well, I hope it comes out in Latin America; I need to see it again, but on a bigger screen!). 

There are many more things that could be analyzed in this film, but this is all I'm going to say for now.

Greasy, grainy, gangrenous cinematography that suggests the image itself entering a state of increasingly fevered degradation, caught in the uncanny between reality and hallucination, the way one might struggle to remember the exact appearance of some strange transmission from the early internet, a rogue signal in the static, at once vivid and indistinct. Primetime’s trance•like effect is not unlike that of a bad dream, which suits the surreal carnival of televised dominance, vigilante justice and public humiliation it observes with such disconcerting psychological proximity. 

It’s specifically a bad dream of the early 2000s, queasily saturated with all the fear, rage, greed and delusion of that era’s politics and entertainment, sickened by their shared impulse to at once profit from punishing others and maintain a moral high ground. The spectacle of performative justice that To Catch a Predator succeeded in televising wouldn’t have been possible without its stakeholders’ maniacal belief that what they were doing was right and just, and this sense of entitlement was heavy in the air. To see Bush’s War on Terror on the television screen shows us what these producers were up against in terms of captivating the public but the awareness of a post-9/11 audience shocked by perceived trespass against them also colors the sickly, retributive catharsis of the pillory that their reality-TV sting-operation series sold to audiences by way of response. 

What makes Primetime transfixing is its smudged and scuzzy visualization of the political fantasy—fittingly, an all-American living room or kitchen that feels stranger and less inhabited the longer you look at it—that this circus of a production required to sustain itself. The alternate reality they imposed was like an abyss, perhaps like a forever war, one that demanded to be fed through greater resources, steeper sacrifices and deeper, darker self-delusion all the time (not to mention the cost to those ensnared, who were destroyed; for what was To Catch a Predator a series where you watch a person realize their life is over). Primetime finds a suitable visual language to express the cognitive dissonance of this production, as well as the false security of such an artificially familiar space as the ones they envisioned when planning their operations; you often feel like you’re watching a production fall under their own show’s hazy spell of entrapment and exposure, or perhaps opening it on the wider world, like Pandora’s box, as if the abyss will seep out into everything as some insidiously abject simulacra of American life. 

Robert Pattinson’s performance in this reflects the tortured, twisted relationship between Chris Hansen and the media personality he projected; and these identities polluting one another until they are inextricable is what Primetime finds as another of its main subjects, showing us how the forces that took this era of television so through the looking glass were present in him individually but also so rife politically they had become endemic, and thus pathological, by the time of his ascendence. Hansen shares our desire for voyeurism and punishment of his perceived enemies, but he also needs to be cast in a positive light, lest his control over the narrative be lessened; the revelations of his exploitative, hypocritical demeanor and inflated ego come as little surprise. What seems to trigger Hansen so losing his grip, and struggling to distinguish between simulation and reality, has to do with his fear of being exposed, of becoming visible in an involuntary and invasive way; Hansen’s public moralizing only suits him when it functions as a one-way mirror, and the implication that he could be ensnared by the fame, money, and attention he seeks hits him with concussive force.

That Primetime destabilizes aesthetically along with Hansen places emphasis on the all-consuming nature of the morass in which these media professionals find themselves, aware that they can no longer claim the morality with which they made their names and waged their war. When the program spirals out of their control, they realize, they’ll also find themselves caught on a camera, the way they’ve proven America is ravenous for. The only solution, they believe, is to double down on catching bigger fish, turning predators into prey and their investigations into televised bloodsport, a seedy national pastime under the guise of a righteous, holy war. That sense of the 2000s as a gladiatorial arena—defined by aggressive ambition, ruthless competition and all-out tabloid warfare, television built around the presentation of urgent, unscripted, unpolished brutality, internet shock sites and nascent video platforms turning people into unwilling combatants for the amusement of an anonymous public—is what comes through most strongly in Primetime. This was the era of vulgar sensationalism, and the woozy, blown-out lighting and sepulchral hues of Primetime are up to the challenge of taking what we all dimly, unhappily recall of its profoundly troubled national temperature.

Parliamo di Primetime il lungometraggio d’esordio di Lance Oppenheim e prodotto da A24.

Il film è ambientato nel 2006 ed è liberalmente ispirato alla storia della messa in onda del programma televisivo americano To Catch a Predator ideato e condotto da Chris Hansen – interpretato da Robert Pattinson .

Il film è la prima opera di finzione di Oppenheim che fino ad adesso era stato un documentarista.

Bene.

La fotografia è desaturata ma dai colori accesi per evocare il look televisivo e l’ansia che permane costantemente nella pellicola.

Tutto è strano e straniante, Pattison è ambiguo e spigoloso.

La realtà che ci viene mostrata è ambigua, del tutto priva di alcun senso morale.

Il regista ha ammesso di essersi ispirato in vari punti alla regia di Manhunter, film del 1982 di Michael Mann.

In entrambi i film si parla di una caccia al mostro: da una parte l’agente Will Graham arriva a mettere a rischio la sua sanità mentale e la sicurezza della sua famiglia nel tentativo di poter comprendere meglio la mentalità del serial killer che sta inseguendo. Dall’altra parte Chris Hansen sembra fin dall’inizio profondamente disturbato, lui è già un predatore ma l’abisso non sembra aver ancora finito con lui.

In tutte e due i film si fa un largo uso di tecnologia di sorveglianza. Quindi tanti monitor, videocamere e innumerevoli strumenti di analisi digitale che non servono solo come oggetti di scena ma che massimizzano questa impressione di straniamento nello spettatore.

David Bolen, il direttore delle luci ha rivelato che le strisce LED blu nella casa-trappola in Texas riprendono l’irrealistica luce che si vedeva spesso nel film precedente e che spiccava per il suo valore ipnotico e straniante.

Infine entrambi parlano dei media e di come la loro presenza cambi i valori all’interno di una indagine della polizia. In Manhunter era tutto esemplificato dalla presenza di un giornalista scandalistico, in Primetime vediamo tutto direttamente attraverso l’occhio della TV. Non si tratta di una vera caccia quanto di innescare una trappola per una preda che sarà estremamente facile catturare.

Il film di Mann era una lunga caduta nell’abisso che diventava sempre più pericoloso e i mostri che lo abitano sempre più familiari. Come aveva mirabilmente scritto Friedrich Nietzsche in Al di là del bene e del male ‘Chi lotta con i mostri deve guardarsi di non diventare, così facendo, un mostro. E se tu scruterai a lungo in un abisso, anche l’abisso scruterà dentro di te’.

Il film di Oppenheim invece potremmo dire che è girato nell’abisso e i personaggi che vediamo non sono certo dei mostri ma alcuni di loro si trovano pericolosamente molto a loro agio li dentro.

In primis il protagonista Chris Hansen che Robert Pattison, a parte forse i primi 15 minuti di film, tratteggia a suon di stranezze.

Al lavoro è il capo ma sembra sempre cercare approvazione anche se non c’è mai l’impressione che  cambierebbe le sue scelte se non l’avesse. Sembra ricercare la perfezione e anche qui di avere l’approvazione altrui ma anche quando la ottiene non sembra bastargli come nella scena in cui  ripete la stessa frase più e più volte con quasi lo stesso tono di voce e inflessione, tutti gli dicono che è perfetto  ma per lui non c’è pace.

Lo  vediamo passare del tempo con il figlio ma c’è una tale distanza e poca naturalezza fra loro al punto che Hansen sembra quasi stare adescando il figlio.

Non va meglio con la moglie con cui c’è soprattutto una strana scena in cui dopo una lunga conversazione su dove stia andando il loro rapporto e che cosa potrà succedere nel futuro prossimo, lui bacia il piede della moglie e tutta la scena è così bizzarra, goffa e inaspettata da avermi creato parecchi dubbi come spettatrice. Cosa ho visto? Boh?

Ma credo che il dubbio mi rimarrà.

Hansen è un uomo strano, quasi un alieno

Cerca il successo, i soldi ma più di tutto cerca quel brivido che prova ogni volta che smaschera uno dei predatori, il potere e il senso di controllo

Per quanto Pattison abbia fatto un buon lavoro credo che all’interno del cast spicchi maggiormente Skyler Gisondo nel ruolo di Dan Plumb un attore di scarso successo perché contraddistinto da una voce e un fisico da ragazzino che però si dimostra utilissimo per To Catch a Predator.

Dan, inizialmente, cerca di mantenere quanta più distanza professionale gli sia permessa nel suo ruolo di esca, lui è li come attore e il suo compito è quello di recitare un ruolo. Lo vediamo provare varie frasi, modulare la voce da ragazzino e studiare la parte, è evidente in lui la soddisfazione per aver trovato un posto e un ruolo in cui lui possa essere la scelta perfetta. Alla fine il suo lavoro all’interno del programma gli varrà il riconoscimento professionale che lui sperava ma il peso di quanto visto e fatto non lo abbandonerà.

Il pubblico non si indentifica con Dan Plumb ma può capirne le motivazioni e perdonare gli errori commessi all’altare di un riconoscimento che non sembrava poter arrivare in alcun altro modo.

Hansen, invece, come il suo programma non può essere capito e non può essere accettato. C’è qualche cosa di quasi alieno nel personaggio e nel suo modo di interagire con gli altri. Non è estrosità fine a se stessa e non è sete di potere è qualche cosa di più strano e malato che guida le azioni del personaggio e che il film si sforza in ogni modo di farci capire che sono sbagliate.

Ed è questo a rendere il film meno di quello che avrebbe potuto essere.

Oppenheim aveva un’opinione ben chiara riguardo al programma To Catch a Predator e non ha permesso al pubblico di farsene una propria e ha preferito imporci la sua.

Tutto è così strano e malato fin  da subito, anche prima di cominciare. Non c’è una discesa nell’abisso perché siamo già lì dopo solo un quarto d’ora di film e lì rimaniamo tutto il tempo.

Non ci sentiamo a casa ovviamente e capiamo che tutto è sbagliato ma c’è qualche  cosa fuori. C’è un fuori?

I started writing this review the same night after I got home from watching the movie, but I kept being too busy to feel like I could finish it. I was originally going to give this a half-hearted 2 stars because the lighting/color grading looked decent, and the idea of printing it on 16 mm film then digitizing it as a visual metaphor for the obfuscation that's come between the audience and the original story was really really interesting but actually spending more time with this movie has only made me more contemptuous.

Based on its promotionals and the responses to it that I’d seen online, I went into the film expecting somewhat of a stylized, in-your-face message about the disconnect between To Catch a Predator’s supposed goals and its methods. People talked about villianization but narratively Hansen is more of a naive crusader swept up in the seedy world of producers/allure of glory than he's an autonomous bad guy. They draw such a linear and resolute line between Hansen's fear of his affair inevitably being revealed, and Hansen’s moments of heightened aggression towards the pedophiles featured on the show, that when he tells Andie she would understand his upset if she had children it felt mostly hollow.

For what the film does depict it makes the same boring choices that “based on a true story” films tend to make when dramatizing real events. Technical details are changed to make timelines feel more urgent/dramatic, the funniest one being that the real forced entry on Conradt’s home happened in clear daylight instead of soppy nighttime.

My biggest issue was what the film didn't show; TCaP filmed the arrests for twenty-three predators in Murphy, Texas leading up to Bill Conradt. In 2007 the Collin County District Attorney's office found that it was not legally viable to pursue indictments for any of these cases.

NBC had also hired an off duty Dallas-metro-area detective named Jimmy Patterson as security. He'd tried to advise the Predator team that the local Texas cops were too under-resourced and inexperienced to handle the show's presence, much less handle going after an assistant district attorney. The producers ignored him and asked to urgently get search and arrest warrants for Conradt's home. The warrant they procured and executed was so rushed that it included the "wrong city, county, and date".

After Conradt's death Patterson was driving out of their decoy location when two Murphy Police Department squad cars pulled him over. The officers had confused Patterson's truck for that of a predator suspect who drove the same color and model, and they physically pulled him out of his vehicle at gunpoint and handcuffed him before realizing their mistake. 

Primetime’s editor has said that the film originally ended on Hansen in shock on Conradt’s lawn, and the final button with Dan getting his SAG card was a late-in-development suggestion by Gisondo. Ajon Singh’s screenplay itself was based on Luke Dittrich’s 2009 Esquire article " Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die " which includes all of the aforementioned information. The idea that a writer could read that article and then produce a script that doesn’t include the part where local police acting on behalf of NBC falsely arrested an off duty officer who was employed by NBC, but instead makes room for Hansen doing air karate alone in the mirror then ends on him standing alone sadly in the grass is batshit to me. I can’t think of a single aspect of this film that deepened the audience’s knowledge of what actually happened with the To Catch a Predator show, nor an artistic element from Singh or Oppenheim that added any substance to the narrative. It wants to be conceptual and heightened, and everything I’ve seen Oppenheim say in regard to this movie seems extremely artistically masturbatory, but this is the same nothingburger fanfare with nothing to actually say that 99% of “based on a true story” films are. With Oppenheim’s documentary background you’d hope he would’ve produced something more interesting within the format. ½ stars
